claims.text: Electrochemical dealloying of a precursor containing noble and less noble metals can produce three-dimensional NM-HEA nanoframeworks.
The resulting NM-HEA nanoframeworks exhibit enhanced catalytic surface features.
A suitable precursor is a near-equiatomic multicomponent alloy containing noble metals and more readily dissolvable sacrificial elements.
Controlled electrochemical dealloying selectively removes the less noble elements from the precursor.
Applied potential, electrolyte, pH, temperature, and reaction time can steer selective dissolution.
The dealloying process can be conducted at ambient or mild temperature.
Selective leaching creates an interconnected porous network.
Residual noble-metal-rich atoms reorganize during selective leaching.
The reorganized framework preserves high entropy and complex surface architectures.
Preferential dissolution of reactive elements creates voids that enable self-organization of the remaining noble-metal atoms into a three-dimensional framework.
Formation of the three-dimensional framework increases exposed surface area.
Dealloying generates diversified active sites beneficial for catalytic reactions.
The dealloyed NM-HEA has greater catalytic efficiency than the undealloyed bulk precursor.
The untreated precursor has a compact bulk microstructure with limited catalytically accessible surface area.
Overly aggressive dealloying can cause structural collapse.
Dealloying conditions that are too mild may generate insufficient porosity.
Excessively high noble-metal content may inhibit sufficient selective dissolution.
Dealloying has been broadly used to create nanoporous structures in noble metals.
Precise atomic control, maintenance of high entropy, dealloying kinetics, and structural reorganization in complex NM-HEAs remain insufficiently optimized.
